notes.h: Hot desert: what defines the biome
notes.b: A biome is a large world region with a distinctive climate, soil and community of plants and animals adapted to those conditions.
points: Climate is the main control: it shapes the soil, and climate and soil together shape the vegetation, which in turn determines which animals can live there.

Biotic inter-relationships: food chains and webs run from producers (plants) to herbivores and carnivores, with decomposers returning nutrients from dead matter to the soil; plants and animals compete for scarce water.

The hot desert is one of the biome belts that follow the world climate belts (tundra, boreal forest, temperate deciduous forest, temperate grassland, Mediterranean, hot desert, savanna, tropical rainforest); on mountains, biomes change with altitude in vertical zones.
Annual rainfall is under 250 mm. Hot deserts lie roughly between 15 and 30 degrees north and south of the equator, mainly on the west sides of continents and in continental interiors.
The Sahara, North Africa, is the world's largest hot desert, at about 9 million km², crossing Morocco, Algeria, Libya, Egypt, Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad and Sudan.

Other hot deserts: the Arabian Desert; the Thar (India and Pakistan); the Namib (south-west Africa); the Atacama (Chile); the Sonoran and Mojave (south-west USA and north-west Mexico); the Great Victoria and Simpson Deserts (Australia).
Map cue: sketch the desert belts on either side of the equator, and label the west coasts of the continents where they reach the sea.
1. Subtropical high pressure: air that rose at the equator sinks at about 30 degrees north and south (the Hadley cell). Sinking air warms and dries, so clouds cannot form.
2. Offshore trade winds blow from the dry interior of the land out over the sea, so they bring no moisture to the coast.

3. Cold ocean currents off west coasts cool the air above them. The cooled lower air is stable (a temperature inversion), so it cannot rise to form rain, and fog forms instead. Examples: the Canary Current (western Sahara), the Benguela Current (Namib), the Humboldt Current (Atacama) and the California Current (Baja California and the Sonoran coast).

4. Rain shadow: mountains force moist air to rise, so it cools and rains on the windward side, then descends dry on the leeward side. The Andes shelter the Atacama from the east; the Sierra Nevada shelters the Mojave, including Death Valley, from Pacific moisture.
5. Continentality: the interior of a large continent is far from the sea, so winds have lost most of their moisture before they arrive.
Summer daytime temperatures often exceed 40 °C.
Clear skies and dry air give intense insolation by day and rapid heat loss by night, so the diurnal (daily) range is very large and nights can be near freezing in winter.
The annual range is larger than in the tropics.
A diurnal range of 20 to 30 °C or more is common.
The highest air temperature officially recognised by the World Meteorological Organization is 56.7 °C, at Furnace Creek, Death Valley, California, on 10 July 1913.

notes.h: Hot desert: rainfall and other climate features
points: Rain is scarce and unreliable. When it falls it is often short, intense convectional downpours that cause flash floods.
Potential evaporation far exceeds rainfall, and humidity is low.
Strong, hot, dusty winds blow across the bare surface.
Coastal fog deserts: the Namib, among the oldest deserts in the world, receives much of its moisture as fog from the cold Benguela Current.
The Atacama, Chile, is the driest non-polar desert on earth; some of its weather stations have recorded no rain for years at a time.
Most of the desert is rock and gravel, not sand dunes.
Hamada: a bare rock plateau. Reg: a stony gravel plain. Erg: a sand sea with dunes.
Wadis are dry river beds that flow only after rain.
Wind erosion landforms are taught in Erosion by wind and are not repeated here.
Aridisols are thin and immature, because weathering is slow without water and is mainly physical.
They are coarse, sandy or stony, with very little humus, so they are pale grey, yellow or red in colour.
Little leaching takes place. Capillary rise brings salts and calcium carbonate to the surface, forming salt crusts (salinisation) and lime hardpans called calcrete or caliche (calcification).
Wind removes fine particles from the surface, leaving a desert pavement of stones.

The soils are alkaline. Where they are irrigated they are fertile, because nutrients have not been leached out; irrigated desert soils are farmed in the Nile valley in Egypt and in California's Imperial Valley, which is irrigated from the Colorado River.
Alluvial soils deposited by rivers that rise outside the desert, such as the Nile, are an exception to the aridisol pattern.
Contrast with rainforest: desert soils are poor in humus but can be fertile when irrigated, whereas rainforest soils stay infertile beneath lush forest.
Cover is sparse, with much bare ground, so biomass and diversity are low.

Plants are widely spaced to reduce competition for water. Creosote bush in the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts limits competitors with evenly spaced plants, roots and chemicals, and individual bushes can be very long-lived.
Vegetation is concentrated along wadis and at oases.
Xerophytes are plants adapted to drought. Succulents store water in their stems or leaves.

Saguaro cactus, found only in the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora, Mexico: its pleated stem expands to store water after rain; it has spines and shallow roots spread widely just below the surface; it can grow over 12 m tall and live over 150 years. Its white flower is the state flower of Arizona.
Cacti are native only to the Americas. Euphorbias in African deserts look similar through convergent evolution.
Spines in place of leaves cut water loss and deter animals; a thick, waxy cuticle reduces evaporation.
Few, sunken stomata; in many succulents they open only at night (Crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, photosynthesis), so less water is lost in the heat of the day.
Long tap roots reach groundwater: mesquite, in the south-west USA and Mexico, has tap roots that can reach tens of metres down.
Shallow, widespread roots catch brief rain.
Acacia trees in the Sahara and Arabian deserts have deep roots, small leaves and thorns.
Small or light-coloured leaves, or leaves shed in drought, reduce water loss.
Welwitschia mirabilis, Namib Desert: it has only two leaves, which grow throughout its life; it absorbs moisture from fog; some plants are thought to be over 1,000 years old.
Halophytes tolerate salty soils. Some plants in coastal deserts harvest moisture from fog.

Ephemerals: their seeds lie dormant for years, then after rain germinate, flower and set seed within weeks, producing a desert bloom. In the Atacama, Chile, a flowering desert (desierto florido) appears in unusually wet years, often linked to El Niño; Death Valley had a widely reported superbloom in 2016.
Dromedary camel, Sahara and Arabia: its hump stores fat, not water. It can go many days without drinking, then drink over 100 litres in a few minutes.
The dromedary camel lets its body temperature rise by several degrees during the day, saving the water that sweating would use, and thick fur on its back shades it from the sun.
The dromedary camel has long eyelashes and closable nostrils that keep out sand, and broad, padded feet that spread its weight on sand.
Very concentrated urine and dry droppings reduce water loss (dromedary camel; kangaroo rat).
Fennec fox, Sahara: the smallest fox, with very large ears that radiate heat; nocturnal; burrows by day; fur on the soles of its feet for hot sand.
Kangaroo rat, North American deserts: gets water from its seed diet and from its metabolism; nocturnal; seals its burrow by day to keep humidity in.
Namib fog-basking beetle: stands head-down on dune crests at dawn so that fog condenses on its back and runs to its mouth.
Thorny devil lizard, Australian deserts: grooves in its skin channel water to its mouth.
Spadefoot toad, Sonoran Desert: estivates (lies dormant) underground through the dry months and emerges after summer rain; its eggs and tadpoles develop extremely quickly, before the pools dry up.
Addax antelope, Sahara: pale coat; gets most of its water from plants; now critically endangered.
Desert locust: breeds rapidly after rain and can form huge swarms.

notes.h: Hot desert: animal and plant relationships
points: Lesser long-nosed bats pollinate saguaro and agave flowers at night.
Gila woodpeckers dig nest holes in saguaros; when the holes are abandoned, elf owls and other birds use them.
Food chains are short, with few producers; seed-eating rodents are prey for snakes, owls and foxes.

notes.h: Hot desert: people and a European example
points: Tuareg (Sahara) and Bedouin (Arabia) are pastoral nomads who herd camels and goats.
Oasis farming grows date palms, whose roots reach groundwater.
Tabernas Desert, Almería province, Andalusia, south-east Spain: often called Europe's only desert, a semi-arid area in the rain shadow of surrounding mountains.
The Tabernas Desert was used as a film set for spaghetti westerns in the 1960s and 1970s.

notes.h: Hot desert: reading a climate graph
points: Annual range: the warmest monthly mean minus the coolest, for example 34 °C minus 12 °C gives an annual range of 22 °C (invented illustrative values).
Total rainfall: the sum of the twelve monthly rainfall bars, for example 150 mm (invented illustrative values); a total under 250 mm points to a hot desert.
Seasonality: describe when the rain falls and when temperatures peak, for example a single short wet season in late summer (invented illustrative values).

notes.h: Tropical rainforest: what defines the biome
notes.b: The tropical rainforest is a biome: a community of plants and animals adapted to a hot, wet equatorial climate and to nutrient-poor soils.
points: Biotic inter-relationships: food chains and webs run from producers to herbivores and carnivores, with decomposers returning nutrients to the soil; species compete for light, and many pollinators and seed dispersers depend on the plants they feed on.
The rainforest is the biome of the equatorial belt, one of the biome belts that follow the world climate belts; mountains show vertical zones of biomes instead.
A dense, evergreen, broadleaved forest in the hot, wet equatorial climate, mainly between about 10 degrees north and south of the equator.
Amazon Basin, South America: the largest, covering about 5.5 million km², with roughly 60% of it in Brazil.
Congo Basin, Central Africa: the second largest, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
South-East Asia: Indonesia (including Sumatra and Borneo), Malaysia and Papua New Guinea.
Smaller areas: Central America, West Africa, eastern Madagascar and north-east Australia (the Daintree, Queensland).
Rainforests cover only about 6% of the earth's land surface but are widely estimated to hold over half of the world's land plant and animal species.
Map cue: shade the equatorial belt, then mark the three main basins and regions.
Mean monthly temperatures are about 26 to 28 °C all year.
The annual range is only about 2 to 3 °C, because the sun stays high and day length barely changes. The sun is overhead at the equator twice a year, at the equinoxes in March and September.
The daily range is greater than the annual range, and there are no seasons in the temperate sense.
Annual rainfall is over 2,000 mm, falling throughout the year and in places far more. Manaus, in the central Amazon, Brazil, receives about 2,300 mm a year.
Stage 1: intense morning heating warms the ground and the moist air above it, which rises.
Stage 2: the rising air cools and cumulonimbus clouds build up.
Stage 3: heavy afternoon thunderstorms follow, almost daily.
The low-pressure belt of rising air along the equator, the ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, also called the doldrums), drives this; some areas have a short drier season when it shifts.
Relative humidity is often over 80%.
A large share of the Amazon's rain is water recycled from the forest by evapotranspiration.

notes.h: Tropical rainforest: soils and the nutrient cycle
points: Latosols are deep, red or yellow, laterised, acidic and infertile, with little humus. Laterisation is explained in Soil processes and the global pattern of soils.
Litter decomposes within weeks in the heat and humidity.
Shallow roots and mycorrhizal fungi (fungi growing on the roots) take up nutrients almost at once and pass them to the trees.
Most nutrients are held in living vegetation rather than the soil, so the nutrient cycle is rapid and closed.
Rainforest soils are infertile despite the lush forest; hot desert soils are infertile in humus but can be fertile when irrigated.
Emergents rise above the canopy, at about 45 to 60 m and more: kapok, the Brazil nut tree in the Amazon, and dipterocarps in South-East Asia.
The canopy, at about 25 to 40 m, is a dense, continuous layer that intercepts most sunlight and rain and holds most of the animal life.
The understorey of young trees and palms reaches up to about 15 m.
The shrub layer grows in the dim light below.
The forest floor is dark and humid; only about 2% of the sunlight reaching the canopy arrives there.
Diagram cue: a labelled vertical profile of the layers, with approximate heights.
Buttress roots support tall trees such as kapok (Ceiba) and the Brazil nut, which have shallow roots.
Shallow roots catch nutrients from the litter layer.
Drip tips and waxy leaves shed heavy rain.
Large leaves in the understorey capture the little light that reaches it.
Thin, smooth bark, because the trunk needs no thick insulation.
Evergreen, with leaves shed and replaced all year. When a tree falls it opens a light gap, and young trees grow rapidly upwards into it.
Lianas are woody climbers, rooted in the soil, that climb trees to reach the light.
Epiphytes such as orchids, bromeliads and ferns grow on branches and take moisture from the air and rain. Bromeliads hold pools of water in their leaf rosettes, which tree frogs use.
Strangler figs start as epiphytes and enclose their host tree.
Pitcher plants (Nepenthes) in the nutrient-poor soils of South-East Asia trap and digest insects.
Rafflesia arnoldii, a parasite on vines in Sumatra and Borneo, has the largest single flower in the world, about 1 m across, and smells of rotting meat to attract flies.
Hundreds of tree species can grow in a single hectare of Amazon rainforest, compared with a handful in an Irish wood.
Many species grow in each hectare, but each species is represented by few individuals.
Most animals live in the canopy (arboreal).
Spider monkeys and howler monkeys, Amazon: prehensile tails used as a fifth limb; howler monkeys are among the loudest land animals.
Three-toed sloth: its very slow metabolism suits a low-energy leaf diet; algae growing in its fur give camouflage; it descends to the ground only about once a week.
Toucan, South and Central America: its large, light bill reaches fruit at the tips of branches and helps it lose heat.
Orangutan, found only in Borneo and Sumatra: the largest tree-living mammal, with long arms.
Harpy eagle, Central and South America: hunts monkeys and sloths in the canopy.
Poison dart frogs, Central and South America: bright colours warn predators of their toxic skin.
Jaguar: the largest cat in the Americas, with a spotted coat for camouflage; a strong swimmer.
Okapi, Congo rainforest: a forest relative of the giraffe, with striped legs for camouflage.
Gorillas and bonobos live in the Congo Basin; bonobos are found only south of the Congo River.
Pollination by insects, birds and bats, and seed dispersal by fruit bats, birds and other animals link plants and animals closely.
Mutualism: Azteca ants live inside Cecropia trees, which give them shelter and food; in return the ants attack herbivores and clear climbing plants from the tree.
Leafcutter ants cut leaves to grow the fungus they eat.
Brazil nut: pollinated mainly by large orchid bees and dispersed by agoutis, rodents that bury the nuts; trees produce poorly in plantations away from intact forest.

notes.h: Tropical rainforest: people of the forest
points: The Yanomami (Brazil and Venezuela border), the Kayapó (Brazilian Amazon) and the Mbuti (Ituri forest, Democratic Republic of the Congo) are hunter-gatherers.
Hunting, gathering and shifting cultivation (slash and burn) at low density let the forest and soil recover. Commercial felling is covered in Human alteration of biomes.
There is no tropical rainforest in Europe. Europe's role in the trade that drives felling is covered in Human alteration of biomes.

notes.h: Tropical rainforest: reading a climate graph
points: Annual range: the warmest monthly mean minus the coolest, for example 28 °C minus 25 °C gives an annual range of 3 °C (invented illustrative values).
Total rainfall: the sum of the twelve monthly rainfall bars, for example 2,400 mm (invented illustrative values); rain falls in every month, with no dry season.
Seasonality: describe the pattern as even, with temperatures near constant through the year (invented illustrative values).

keyTerms.definition: A thin, immature desert soil with very little humus, in which salts or lime are often brought up near the surface.
The circulation in which air rising at the equator sinks at about 30 degrees north and south, warming and drying as it descends.
The dry leeward side of a mountain, where air that has dropped its rain on the windward side descends and warms.
The difference between the highest and lowest temperature in one day.
A plant adapted to survive long periods of drought.
A plant that stores water in its stems or leaves.
A plant whose seeds lie dormant until rain, then germinate, flower and seed within weeks.
Dormancy through the hottest and driest part of the year.
A bare rock plateau in a hot desert.
A sand sea of dunes.
A dry river bed that flows only after rain.
A surface of stones left behind when wind has removed the fine particles.
A hard layer of lime (calcium carbonate) formed near the surface where capillary rise has brought it up.
A plant that tolerates salty soils.
A deep, red or yellow, acidic rainforest soil that is laterised and infertile.
The process in which heavy rainfall leaches silica and other minerals from the soil, leaving iron and aluminium oxides behind.
Fungi that grow on plant roots and pass nutrients to the plant.
A tree that rises above the main canopy of the rainforest.
A woody climber, rooted in the soil, that climbs trees to reach light.
A plant that grows on the branches of other plants and takes moisture from the air and rain.
Rain formed when intense heating makes moist air rise, cool and condense into storm clouds.
The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, a low-pressure belt of rising air along the equator.
The loss of water to the atmosphere from both evaporation and the transpiration of plants.
A relationship in which two species each gain from the other.

factCards.term: Hot desert biome: location and named deserts
factCards.definition: Under 250 mm of rain a year, about 15–30° N and S, mainly on west sides and in continental interiors. The Sahara (about 9 million km²) is the largest; others are the Arabian, Thar, Namib, Atacama, Sonoran, Mojave, Great Victoria and Simpson Deserts.

factCards.term: Hot desert: five causes of aridity
factCards.definition: Subtropical high pressure, where sinking air warms so clouds cannot form; offshore trade winds from the dry interior; cold ocean currents that make the air stable, giving fog not rain; rain shadow behind mountains; continentality, far from the sea.

factCards.term: Hot deserts: match each to its cold current or rain shadow
factCards.definition: Canary Current: western Sahara. Benguela Current: Namib. Humboldt Current: Atacama. California Current: Baja California and the Sonoran coast. The Andes shelter the Atacama; the Sierra Nevada shelters the Mojave, including Death Valley.

factCards.term: Hot desert temperature: characteristics and the world record
factCards.definition: Summer days often exceed 40 °C; clear, dry air gives a diurnal range of 20–30 °C or more, with winter nights near freezing. Record: 56.7 °C at Furnace Creek, Death Valley, 10 July 1913 (WMO); the 58 °C El Azizia reading was rejected in 2012.

factCards.term: Hot desert rainfall: characteristics and two extreme deserts
factCards.definition: Rain is scarce and unreliable, often in short, intense convectional downpours causing flash floods; evaporation far exceeds rainfall. The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert; the Namib gets much of its moisture as fog from the cold Benguela Current.

factCards.term: Aridisols: characteristics and when they become fertile
factCards.definition: Thin and immature (slow, mainly physical weathering); coarse, with little humus, so pale grey, yellow or red; little leaching, so capillary rise leaves salt crusts and calcrete; alkaline. Fertile when irrigated, as in the Nile valley and the Imperial Valley.

factCards.term: Saguaro cactus: where it grows, three adaptations and its size and age
factCards.definition: Only in the Sonoran Desert (Arizona and Sonora, Mexico). Its pleated stem expands to store water after rain; spines replace leaves; shallow roots spread widely just below the surface; it can grow over 12 m tall and live over 150 years.

factCards.term: Desert plants: four ways leaves and stems cut water loss
factCards.definition: Spines in place of leaves, which also deter animals; a thick, waxy cuticle; few, sunken stomata that in many succulents open only at night (CAM photosynthesis); small or light-coloured leaves, or leaves shed in drought.

factCards.term: Desert plants: root and life-cycle strategies, with named plants
factCards.definition: Mesquite tap roots reach tens of metres to groundwater; acacias have deep roots, small leaves and thorns; ephemerals bloom within weeks of rain, as in the Atacama's flowering desert in wet El Niño years and Death Valley's superbloom of 2016.

factCards.term: Welwitschia and creosote bush: what makes each special
factCards.definition: Welwitschia mirabilis (Namib): only two leaves, which grow throughout its life; absorbs fog moisture; some are thought to be over 1,000 years old. Creosote bush (Mojave, Sonoran): evenly spaced plants whose roots and chemicals limit competitors.

factCards.term: Dromedary camel: five adaptations to the desert
factCards.definition: Its hump stores fat, not water; it can go days without drinking, then drink over 100 litres in minutes; its body temperature rises by day to save sweat; long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep out sand; broad, padded feet spread its weight.

factCards.term: Fennec fox and kangaroo rat: how each survives the desert
factCards.definition: Fennec fox (Sahara): the smallest fox; very large ears radiate heat; nocturnal; burrows; furry soles for hot sand. Kangaroo rat (North America): gets water from seeds and its metabolism, has very concentrated urine, and seals its burrow by day.

factCards.term: Desert animals: three ways to get or save water
factCards.definition: The Namib fog-basking beetle stands head-down on dunes at dawn so fog runs to its mouth; the thorny devil lizard's skin grooves channel water to its mouth; the spadefoot toad estivates underground and its tadpoles develop before pools dry up.

factCards.term: Hot desert: biotic inter-relationships with named species
factCards.definition: Lesser long-nosed bats pollinate saguaro and agave flowers at night; Gila woodpeckers dig nest holes in saguaros that elf owls later use; food chains are short, and seed-eating rodents are prey for snakes, owls and foxes.

factCards.term: Tabernas Desert: Europe's example of a desert
factCards.definition: In Almería province, Andalusia, south-east Spain: semi-arid badlands in the rain shadow of surrounding mountains, often called Europe's only desert; a film set for spaghetti westerns in the 1960s and 1970s.

factCards.term: Tropical rainforest biome: location and main regions
factCards.definition: Mainly within about 10° of the equator. The Amazon Basin is largest (about 5.5 million km², roughly 60% in Brazil); then the Congo Basin; then South-East Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea); smaller areas include the Daintree, Queensland.

factCards.term: Rainforest biodiversity: key figures
factCards.definition: Rainforests cover only about 6% of the earth's land but are widely estimated to hold over half of its land plant and animal species. Hundreds of tree species can grow in one hectare of Amazon forest, against a handful in an Irish wood.

factCards.term: Rainforest temperature: figures and why it barely changes
factCards.definition: Monthly means about 26–28 °C, an annual range of only about 2–3 °C, because the sun is always high (overhead at the equinoxes in March and September) and day length barely changes. The daily range exceeds the annual range; there is no summer or winter season.

factCards.term: Rainforest rainfall: amount and the daily convection cycle
factCards.definition: Over 2,000 mm a year (Manaus about 2,300 mm). Morning heating makes moist air rise; it cools and cumulonimbus build; heavy afternoon thunderstorms follow almost daily, driven by the ITCZ. Humidity is often over 80% and much rain is recycled from the forest.

factCards.term: Rainforest nutrient cycle: how lush forest grows on infertile soil
factCards.definition: Latosols are acidic with little humus, but litter decomposes within weeks, and shallow roots and mycorrhizal fungi take up nutrients almost at once. Most nutrients are held in the living vegetation, so the cycle is rapid and closed.

factCards.term: Rainforest layers: heights and features of each
factCards.definition: Emergents about 45–60 m or more (kapok, Brazil nut, dipterocarps); dense canopy about 25–40 m, holding most animal life; understorey up to about 15 m; shrub layer; dark forest floor getting about 2% of the sunlight that reaches the canopy.

factCards.term: Rainforest trees: five adaptations to the climate and soil
factCards.definition: Buttress roots support tall, shallow-rooted trees such as kapok and Brazil nut; shallow roots catch nutrients from litter; drip tips and waxy leaves shed heavy rain; large understorey leaves catch dim light; thin, smooth bark, as no insulation is needed.

factCards.term: Rainforest climbers, epiphytes and plants of poor soils: named examples
factCards.definition: Lianas climb trees to the light; epiphytes such as orchids and bromeliads grow on branches; strangler figs enclose their host; pitcher plants (Nepenthes) digest insects; Rafflesia arnoldii, a parasite, has the largest flower, about 1 m across.

factCards.term: Rainforest canopy animals: adaptations of five named species
factCards.definition: Spider and howler monkeys: prehensile tails as a fifth limb. Three-toed sloth: slow metabolism suits a leaf diet; algae in its fur camouflage it. Toucan: large, light bill reaches fruit. Orangutan (Borneo, Sumatra only): largest tree-living mammal, long arms.

factCards.term: Rainforest animals: camouflage, warning colours and predators
factCards.definition: Poison dart frogs' bright colours warn of toxic skin; the jaguar, the largest cat in the Americas, has a spotted, camouflaged coat and swims strongly; the okapi of the Congo has striped legs for camouflage; the harpy eagle hunts monkeys and sloths.

factCards.term: Rainforest mutualism: three named examples
factCards.definition: Azteca ants live in Cecropia trees, which give shelter and food, and attack herbivores and climbers; leafcutter ants grow the fungus they eat; the Brazil nut needs orchid bees to pollinate it and agoutis to bury its nuts, so it yields poorly in plantations.

factCards.term: Rainforest peoples: three named groups and how they used the forest
factCards.definition: The Yanomami (Brazil–Venezuela border), Kayapó (Brazilian Amazon) and Mbuti (Ituri forest, Democratic Republic of the Congo). Hunting, gathering and shifting cultivation at low density let the forest and soil recover.

questions.prompt: With reference to one biome you have studied, account for its climate and explain how this climate affects its soils and vegetation.
questions.model: Hot desert only. Climate: subtropical high pressure sinks at about 30 degrees, warming and drying so clouds cannot form; offshore trade winds blow from the interior; cold currents such as the Benguela cool the air and produce fog rather than rain; mountains such as the Andes create a rain shadow; continentality keeps the interior dry. Result: rainfall under 250 mm, unreliable and often falling as flash-flood downpours; summer daytime temperatures often over 40 °C; a very large diurnal range; potential evaporation far exceeds rainfall. Soils: aridisols that are thin and immature because weathering is slow without water; very little humus; capillary rise brings salts and calcium carbonate to the surface, forming salt crusts and calcrete; desert pavement where wind has removed the fine particles. Vegetation: sparse, widely spaced plants with low biomass; adaptations include the saguaro's pleated stem and shallow roots, the mesquite's tap roots, the thick waxy cuticle and few sunken stomata of succulents, and ephemerals that bloom within weeks of rain. One bridging point may note an animal adaptation, such as the dromedary camel's fat store, and no further animal detail.

questions.prompt: Examine the characteristics of one biome you have studied with reference to climate, soils and fauna.
questions.model: Tropical rainforest only, in three aspects. Climate: an equatorial climate with temperatures of about 26 to 28 °C, an annual range of only 2 to 3 °C, and rainfall over 2,000 mm from convectional storms driven by the ITCZ; Manaus receives about 2,300 mm. Soils: latosols that are deep, red, laterised, acidic and infertile; litter decomposes within weeks and mycorrhizal fungi pass nutrients to the trees, so most nutrients are held in living vegetation. Fauna: most animals are arboreal; named adaptations include the three-toed sloth's slow metabolism and algae camouflage, the howler monkey's prehensile tail, the toucan's bill, which helps it lose heat, and the orangutan's long arms; biotic inter-relationships include Brazil nut pollination by orchid bees, dispersal by agoutis, and leafcutter ants farming fungus.

questions.prompt: Describe the climatic and soil characteristics of one biome and examine their impact on the development of vegetation.
questions.model: Tropical rainforest only. Climate and soil: a hot, wet equatorial climate with a small temperature range and high convectional rainfall; latosols with a rapid nutrient cycle through shallow roots and fungi. Vegetation development: the layered structure, from emergents of 45 to 60 m and more, through the canopy at about 25 to 40 m and the understorey, to the dark forest floor, which receives about 2% of the sunlight reaching the canopy. Plant adaptations: buttress roots, shallow roots, drip tips, waxy leaves, large understorey leaves, lianas, epiphytes, strangler figs, and an evergreen habit with rapid growth into light gaps.
